note: Covers Model Context Protocol tool poisoning and RAG poisoning, and maps defences to OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025.
title: Prompt Injection Attacks in Large Language Models and AI Agent Systems: A Comprehensive Review of Vulnerabilities, Attack Vectors, and Defense Mechanisms
explain_beginner: As AI chatbots get connected to email inboxes, code editors, and company databases through tools and plugins, a specific kind of attack called prompt injection has become a serious practical problem, where hidden instructions planted in a document, webpage, or email trick the AI into ignoring its original task and doing something the attacker wants instead. Gulyamov and coauthors reviewed dozens of real, documented cases of this happening, not just theoretical demonstrations, including one case where hidden instructions in a connected tool led to a security flaw serious enough to receive one of the most severe official vulnerability ratings, and another where a booby-trapped PDF caused a connected AI system to damage physical industrial equipment. They found that poisoning just five carefully crafted documents in a knowledge base an AI searches through could successfully manipulate its answers the vast majority of the time. The review's sobering conclusion is that no single fix reliably solves this, the authors argue the problem is baked into how these AI systems process instructions and untrusted text using the same channel, so multiple overlapping defenses are needed, and even then, complete protection may not be achievable with current AI designs.
explain_business: For any organization deploying an AI agent that reads external content, emails, webpages, uploaded documents, connected databases, or tools through a protocol like MCP, this review documents that the realistic risk is not hypothetical, it cites a Copilot vulnerability rated 9.6 out of 10 in severity and a case where a poisoned PDF triggered real damage to physical industrial equipment through a connected AI system, alongside a retrieval augmented system where just five poisoned documents in a knowledge base achieved a 90 percent manipulation success rate. The direct operational implication is that any AI agent with tool access or document retrieval capability should be treated as running in an environment with a wide, difficult to fully close attack surface, meriting layered defenses like the PALADIN framework's input isolation, sandboxing, and anomaly detection working together, mapped against OWASP's LLM security guidance, rather than a single vendor provided safety filter. Because the authors themselves argue complete architectural protection is not currently achievable, procurement and security teams should budget for ongoing monitoring and incident response specifically for prompt injection, not treat it as a one time configuration task, for any AI system connected to untrusted external content today.
explain_practitioner: This review synthesizes 45 sources plus documented security incidents from 2023 to 2025 into a taxonomy covering direct jailbreaking through role play and encoding tricks, indirect injection through poisoned external content like webpages and emails, tool poisoning through malicious descriptions embedded in Model Context Protocol servers including delayed activation rug pull attacks, and RAG poisoning, where the authors report five adversarially crafted documents seeded into a retrieval corpus achieved a 90 percent attack success rate. Documented real world incidents cited include a GitHub Copilot vulnerability, CVE-2025-53773, rated 9.6 out of 10 in severity for enabling remote code execution, and a supply chain style attack the authors call CamoLeak that exfiltrated private repository secrets by bypassing content security policy protections. The authors propose PALADIN, a five layer defense in depth framework spanning input isolation, sandboxed execution, prompt hardening, behavioral anomaly detection, and RAG specific integrity checks, mapped explicitly to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025. Their stated limitation is architectural, they argue that because large language models process trusted instructions and untrusted data through the same text channel with no hard syntactic boundary, a purely semantic defense can in principle always be bypassed through further social engineering of the prompt.
